how.title: How to Use This Handbook
intro: This handbook is written to be worked through, not only read. It is organised into twelve sections, each covering one area of management practice, and each ending with a Section Review made up of three parts.
A section read and not reviewed will change very little.

cards.title: The Ship
cards.text: A short panel opening each section, putting it in a ship’s terms, with one question to take back to your own work.

cards.title: Ten tests
cards.text: Self-tests at the end of every section. A “no” is more useful than a “yes”.

cards.title: Questions for discussion
cards.text: For the group session, or for a colleague.

cards.title: Practical exercise
cards.text: One task to carry back into real work before the next session.

who.title: Who This Handbook Is For
who.intro: It is written for anyone who is answerable for work that other people do, or who is about to be. No prior study of management is assumed and no qualification is needed to use it. The examples are drawn from charity, education and administrative settings, but the principles are not sector-specific.
head: Reader
What this handbook gives them
rows: A complete first grounding — what the job actually consists of, and what to do in the first months
Experienced managers with no formal training
A structure and a vocabulary for what they already do by instinct, and the gaps made visible
The systems half of the work: documentation, control, discipline and policy
Delegation, decisions, meetings, mentoring and handling poor performance
Policy, levels of authority, and organisational structure
What to expect of the managers they appoint, and where the board’s own line falls
A ready participant text for a sixteen-session course, with self-tests and exercises
The working reality of management, rather than the theory of it, before the first post
How responsibility, authority and accountability work in an unpaid setting
who.outro: It will be of least use to anyone looking for a quick reference to dip into. The sections are cumulative: each assumes the one before it.

ship.title: The Ship

card.title: The Ship
card.caption: A vessel that carries people who could not make the crossing alone.

paras: The programme is built around one image, and it is the one the centre is named for. As Safinah — السفينة — is the ship.

A ship is the oldest working example of what this handbook is about: a group of people, a finite store of resources, a hostile environment, a destination, and one person answerable for whether they arrive. Everything management does has a counterpart on board. Planning is charting a course. Structure is the ship’s company. Discipline is the watch and the bell. Policy is standing orders. Control is the sounding line.

Every section opens with a short panel called The Ship, which puts that section’s subject in these terms and ends with one question to take back to your own vessel. The panels are not decoration. If you can explain a section to somebody in the ship’s terms, you have understood it; if you cannot, go back.
The image carries one more thing. A ship is a vessel that carries people who could not make the crossing alone. That is the work.

room.title: The Management Room: Twelve Pathways
paras: This wheel hangs in the Management room at As Safinah. It shows the twelve pathways — the courses, practice and support — offered in the room, from Foundations at the top, reading clockwise.

The pathways draw on the sections of this handbook throughout: Foundations on Section 1, Planning and Priorities on Section 3, Delegation on Section 4, Coaching and Supervision on Section 5, and so on. Use the wheel to find your way into the handbook from the room, and the handbook to go deeper than any one session can.
